record.paper_title: The 1999 Heineman Prize Address Integrable models in statistical mechanics: The hidden field with unsolved problems
record.original_question: For the integrable chiral Potts model with N >= 3 states per site, can Baxter's free-energy method be extended so that one can determine the complete eigenvalue spectrum of the transfer matrix on the higher-genus spectral curve, despite the absence of the algebraic-geometric machinery that solves the analogous genus-one Ising case?

evidence.quote: Most unhappily, however, for the higher genus case the analogous solution requires machinery from algebraic geome�toy which does not exist. For the problem of the free energy Baxter [40] has devised an ingenious method of solution which bypasses algebraic geometry completely but even here some problems remain in extending the method to the complete eigenvalue spectrum [41].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the integrable chiral Potts model on a two-dimensional lattice with N ≥ 3 states per site, whose Boltzmann weights are parametrized by points on the chiral Potts spectral curve

  k' (1 - x^N) = (1 - k x^N)^{1/2}(1 - k y^N)^{1/2},  μ^N = (1 - k x^N)/(1 - k y^N),

a smooth algebraic curve of genus g = N^3 - 2N^2 + 1 (which exceeds 1 for N ≥ 3). Let T(p) denote the row-to-row transfer matrix of this model, depending on the spectral parameter p = (x,y,μ) lying on the curve. For the genus-one Ising case (N = 2) the complete eigenvalue spectrum of T(p) is obtained via classical algebraic-geometric machinery (theta functions on an elliptic curve). For N ≥ 3 such machinery on higher-genus curves is not available in the form needed; however, the bulk free energy

  f(p) = − lim_{M,L→∞} (ML)^{-1} log Λ_max(p)

has been computed by a functional-equation / "broken rapidity line" method that bypasses algebraic geometry.

Problem: Determine whether this functional-equation approach to the free energy can be extended to yield the complete eigenvalue spectrum of the chiral Potts transfer matrix T(p) for all N ≥ 3 on the full higher-genus spectral curve (not merely at the superintegrable specialization), giving every eigenvalue as an explicit analytic function of p on the curve.
artifact.category_tag: Chiral Potts model / integrable lattice models
artifact.status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made since 1999. Baxter, using functional relations and the broken-rapidity-line technique (following Bazhanov–Stroganov and Jimbo et al.), derived eigenvalues of the chiral Potts transfer matrix for the superintegrable case and later extended the method to compute the order parameter and partition-function-related quantities on the higher-genus curve. The complete eigenvalue spectrum on the full curve for general (non-superintegrable) parameters, however, does not appear to have been fully obtained in closed analytic form; results so far are restricted to special slices or rely on functional equations whose complete solution set is not fully characterized. The problem is therefore best classified as partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Eigenvalue Spectrum of the Superintegrable Chiral Potts Model
status_evidence.snippet: Eigenvalues of the superintegrable chiral Potts model derived via functional relations.
status_evidence.claim: Complete spectrum known in the superintegrable specialization.

status_evidence.title: The Order Parameter of the Chiral Potts Model
status_evidence.snippet: Baxter (2005) proved the order-parameter conjecture using functional equations and the broken-rapidity-line technique on the high-genus chiral Potts curve.
status_evidence.claim: Functional-equation method has been extended beyond the free energy to other quantities.

status_evidence.title: Chiral Potts model — Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The weights are parametrized by a high-genus curve; standard corner transfer matrix and algebraic-geometric machinery do not apply directly.
status_evidence.claim: Higher-genus difficulty noted; general spectrum on full curve not fully resolved.
